prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, opening the 10^-18 regime of frequency measurement.

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep optical lattice clocks as my single preferred part. Five of eight members now name it first, but I weigh the science rather than the count. The chair asks what the citation recognises that the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for single quantum systems did not. My answer is the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice: a many-atom trapping scheme in which the light shift of the clock transition cancels, so that very large atom numbers can be interrogated without the perturbation that limits a single trapped ion. That is a distinct conceptual step, not a refinement of the comb or of ion control, and it is what allowed stability and accuracy near 10^-18 to be reached. The credit is concentrated and defensible, Katori for the concept and first demonstration and Ye for taking the strontium lattice clock to the accuracy and stability frontier, and the result is independently reproduced in several national laboratories. I do not regard the unreached redefinition of the second as a reason to wait, because the performance and its use in relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants are already established.
statement.case_against: The novelty margin against the 2005 and 2012 prizes is real, and the citation must be built strictly around the neutral-atom lattice and its realisation, not around precision metrology in general. Two names omit Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the theory of Derevianko, and I cannot show that this omission is costless; I judge it defensible because the concept and the record-performance realisation are the two separable contributions. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and a prize after it would be easier to justify on practical impact, though not on scientific content.

responses.point: Kroll supports B002 with a Katori-Ye allocation, and asks whether his research stay in Hall's laboratory, with Ye associated with that group at JILA, should lead him to abstain.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and the maturity argument, and I hold that the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly, as you and Olsson both say. On your disclosure, the link is a historical laboratory association and not a collaboration with Ye or a stake in the outcome. I would record it and not require abstention, but it is for the chair and the committee to decide, and the vote on B002 should be read with that note attached. My own support does not depend on yours, which is why I ground it in the novelty argument above.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and says he could accept B002 as the second part of a two-part prize, arguing that moire flat bands changed what can be asked of correlated matter.
responses.response: I take the conceptual-novelty argument seriously and I do not dispute that the prediction-then-discovery pairing is the cleanest in condensed matter. I do not move on maturity: the flat-band origin is settled, but the pairing mechanism is not, and eight years is short. A two-part prize would also let the weaker of the two cases dilute the stronger. I would rather the committee decide B038 in a later year with the mechanism clearer, and I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B038 and argues that the citation can be worded around the discovery and the platform, leaving the pairing mechanism outside, while conceding that clocks are the safer choice if maturity outweighs breadth.
responses.response: Leaving the mechanism out of the citation answers part of my concern, and it is a fair drafting solution. It does not remove the experimental-credit problem you note, since Cao and the early authors do much of the bench work. I agree with your own formulation that if maturity is weighted above breadth the clocks are the safer choice, and that is how I weigh it. I would call the clocks the more complete achievement, and moire graphene the more promising one.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps the experimental Higgs discovery first but identifies attribution as the decisive weakness, and names B002 and B038 as the better-attributed alternatives.
responses.response: The scientific case is beyond dispute and I would not be surprised by a later Higgs prize. I still see no principled three-name rule for a discovery made by two collaborations; founding leaders, discovery-year spokespersons and analysis conveners each give a different trio. Your own statement that B002 and B038 are better attributed is the one I rely on. If you or others propose a rule that the committee can defend in the citation, I will read it, but I cannot rank B053 first without one.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from IceCube to B002 and records that Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Wineland-group ion clocks have real claims that a Katori-Ye prize passes over.
responses.response: I agree the omissions are real, and I would put the answer to the chair's question this way: the committee should credit the two separable contributions, the concept with its first demonstration and the record-accuracy realisation, and accept that the citation will not name everyone. On IceCube I accept the 2013 diffuse flux as firm, but the interpretation is still forming, so I treat it as a discovery in progress. I note that you list it as an alternative, which is a reasonable place for it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes.
Whether a Katori-Ye allocation is fair against Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Derevianko, and whether anyone has a better two-name or three-name allocation than the one supplied.
Whether the committee wants a second part, and if so whether B038 would be mature enough in a later year.
If circuit QED is revisited, how to resolve Blais versus Girvin within three seats, and how much the 2025 prize should count against it.
statement.conflict_note: I am director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a Chalmers professor working on circuit and waveguide QED. Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and my frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum work in superconducting circuits, and Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. This is a connection to circuit QED (B017), listed here only as an alternative, and I would recuse myself from any decision that places B017 above B002. I note Olsson's disclosure that I am also at Chalmers. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B002 or B038, and nothing in it changes since round 1. I have no documented link to Katori or Ye.
